metadata.title: Evansville, Indiana — steam-road hub
metadata.note: The six railroads that radiated from Evansville in 1900, plus the two twentieth-century additions (the Big Four’s Mount Carmel line of 1911). Evansville was one of the larger rail centres of the lower Midwest and had no coverage in this map at all; the nearest existing feature was 46 km away. Features are split at ownership changes per Rule 4, so most corridors appear twice or three times with identical geometry and different companies/colours. Electric lines — the city streetcars, the Evansville Suburban and Newburgh, and the Evansville and Ohio Valley interurbans — are NOT in this file; none of them survive in OpenStreetMap and they need street-grid tracing.
metadata.geometry_method: Corridor-constrained shortest path over OpenStreetMap ways filtered on old_railway_operator (C&EI, L&N, Southern, NYC, IC), which is well populated across south-west Indiana. Every feature carries its own geometry_quality naming its traced length, the documented mileage where one is known, and every straight-line leg.
not_yet_sourced: Last passenger train on the Evansville–Terre Haute line of the Evansville, Indianapolis and Terre Haute (Big Four). The drawn end year of 1942 is borrowed from the Big Four’s Mount Carmel line and is unverified.
Last passenger train on the Illinois Central’s Evansville–Olney (ex-PD&E) line. 1938 is inferred from a source that dates the last passenger train on the Peoria–Mattoon end to the "late 1930s".
Whether Southern Railway passenger service between Louisville and Princeton ended with the June 1953 Princeton–St. Louis discontinuance or on a different date.
Every headway_min and avg_speed_kmh in this file is an estimate; no Official Guide or company timetable was consulted for any segment.
The PD&E north of Olney (Newton–Mattoon–Decatur–Peoria) is not drawn at all — the grade is gone and is not mapped in OSM.
metadata.freight_only_audit: Rule 1 check: nothing freight-only was added. The Evansville Belt Railway, the Algers Winslow and Western, and the modern Evansville Western / Indiana Southern / Indiana Southwestern short lines were all deliberately left out. Where a corridor outlived its passenger service the feature ends at the passenger date and the note says what happened afterwards.
metadata.horsecar_audit: Rule 5 check: no animal-powered operation is drawn; every feature here is a steam railroad.

properties.line: Evansville and Terre Haute: Evansville – Terre Haute
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=C&EI (CSX CE&D Subdivision and its abandoned sections) by corridor-constrained shortest path through Princeton, Vincennes and Sullivan. Traced length 108.2 mi against a documented 109 mi (Evansville–Vincennes 51 + Vincennes–Terre Haute 58). No straight-line approximation longer than 1.2 km. Drawn on the surviving alignment, which is the same one the E&TH used.
properties.speed_source: Estimated. No timetable was consulted; 45 km/h is a general figure for a 19th-century Indiana trunk line.

segments.note: Opened as the Evansville and Crawfordsville Railroad: through traffic to Vincennes and on to Terre Haute from 23 November 1853, completed 1854. Renamed Evansville and Terre Haute Railroad in 1877. Headway is an estimate for a mid-century trunk line, not a timetable figure.
sources: Segment-level: opening and 1877 rename from the Evansville and Crawfordsville Railroad article.

segments.note: Evansville and Terre Haute Railroad. Absorbed into the Chicago and Eastern Illinois in 1911; the post-1911 years are drawn as a separate C&EI feature on the same geometry. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1877 rename and 1911 consolidation into the C&EI.

properties.speed_source: Estimated for a 20th-century secondary main line; no timetable consulted.

segments.note: C&EI Evansville Division, the southern end of the Chicago–Evansville main line. Carried the "Whippoorwill" (Chicago–Evansville) and the C&EI section of the L&N "Georgian". Passenger service ended when Amtrak took over on 1 May 1971 and did not include Evansville. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: C&EI Chicago–Evansville passenger service and its 1971 end.

properties.line: Evansville, Henderson and Nashville: Henderson – Nashville
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=L&N (CSX Henderson Subdivision and the Nashville Terminal Subdivision) through Madisonville, Hopkinsville, Guthrie and Springfield. Traced length 144.0 mi Henderson–Nashville; largest straight-line bridge 2.15 km. This is the surviving alignment, which is the one the EH&N built.
properties.speed_source: Estimated. No L&N timetable was consulted.

segments.note: Opened April 1871, built by Evansville business interests for a direct line south. Drawn from Henderson, not Evansville: the Ohio River was not bridged until 1885 and Evansville passengers crossed by ferry. Acquired by the St. Louis and Southeastern in 1872. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1871 opening and 1872 acquisition by the StL&SE.

properties.line: St. Louis and Southeastern: Henderson – Nashville

properties.speed_source: Estimated. No L&N timetable was consulted.

segments.note: Operated as the StL&SE Kentucky Division. Still Henderson–Nashville only; the Evansville bridge came in 1885. Leased to the L&N on 1 May 1880. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: StL&SE ownership 1872–1880 and the 1 May 1880 L&N lease.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=L&N (CSX Henderson Subdivision and the Nashville Terminal Subdivision) through Madisonville, Hopkinsville, Guthrie and Springfield. properties.speed_source: Estimated. No L&N timetable was consulted.

segments.note: L&N St. Louis Division / Henderson Subdivision, part of the Chicago–Florida "Dixie Route" once the Evansville bridge opened in 1885. The last regularly scheduled passenger train reached Evansville on 30 April 1971; Amtrak did not pick up the route. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1880 L&N lease and the 30 April 1971 last train.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM L&N-tagged ways (CSX Evansville Terminal and Henderson Subdivisions). 12.7 mi, no bridging longer than 0.6 km. Drawn on the modern bridge alignment, which is the 1885 crossing rebuilt in place.
properties.speed_source: Estimated; a terminal-approach figure, not a timetable speed.

segments.note: The Ohio River bridge at Henderson opened in 1885 and put Evansville on the L&N system; before that, southbound passengers ferried across. Drawn separately from the Henderson–Nashville trunk because the trunk carried passengers from 1871 and this link did not exist until 1885. Ended with the last train on 30 April 1971. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1885 Ohio River bridge; 1971 end of service.

properties.line: St. Louis and Southeastern: Evansville – East St. Louis
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=L&N (today’s Evansville Western Railway) for the first 146.2 mi, Evansville to near Lebanon, Illinois. THE LAST 15.5 mi INTO EAST ST. LOUIS IS AN APPROXIMATION: no OSM way in that terminal area carries the L&N tag, so it follows rails in the same corridor that are tagged to other companies. Total traced 161.8 mi. Largest straight-line bridge 2.45 km. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 10 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).
properties.speed_source: Estimated for an 1870s prairie main line; no timetable consulted.

segments.note: Chartered 1869 to link East St. Louis with Evansville and opened in late 1871, reaching Evansville from Mount Vernon, Illinois. Reorganized as the South East and St. Louis Railway and leased to the L&N on 1 May 1880. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1869 charter, late-1871 opening, 1 May 1880 L&N lease.

properties.company: Louisville, Evansville and St. Louis Railroad
properties.line: Louisville, Evansville and St. Louis: Evansville – Huntingburg
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=Southern and named "Evansville Branch" — a single connected chain, 47.4 mi Evansville to Huntingburg, largest straight-line bridge 1.19 km.
properties.speed_source: Estimated for an 1880s Indiana line; no timetable consulted.

segments.note: The "Air Line" reached Evansville as part of the New Albany–Mount Vernon, Illinois main line opened in 1882. Consolidated as the Louisville, Evansville and St. Louis Consolidated Railway in 1889, into receivership 1894, and into the Southern Railway on 1 January 1901. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1882 opening, 1889 consolidation, 1 January 1901 transfer to the Southern.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=Southern and named "Evansville Branch" — a single connected chain, 47.4 mi Evansville to Huntingburg, largest straight-line bridge 1.19 km.

segments.note: Southern Railway St. Louis Division. Under the Southern this became a branch off the Princeton main line rather than the through route. Passenger service on the Evansville branch ended in April 1939. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: Southern takeover 1901 and the April 1939 end of Evansville branch passenger service.

properties.line: Louisville, Evansville and St. Louis: Huntingburg – New Albany
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=Southern ("Southern-East District"), 68.6 mi Huntingburg to New Albany, largest straight-line bridge 1.31 km. Stops at New Albany: the Ohio River crossing into Louisville over the K&I bridge is NOT drawn, so the line is about 4 mi short of Louisville Union Station.

segments.note: Eastern half of the "Air Line" main, New Albany to Huntingburg, opened 1882. Trains ran through to Louisville over the Ohio River bridge at New Albany. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1882 opening of the New Albany–Mount Vernon main line.

segments.note: Southern Railway St. Louis Division main line. Southern ended the Princeton–St. Louis through passenger run in June 1953; the Louisville end is drawn to the same year. Headway estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: June 1953 is documented for the Princeton–St. Louis run; whether the Louisville–Princeton portion ended in the same month was not checked.

sources: Segment-level: 1872 Princeton–Albion opening and the 1882 through main line.

properties.line: Evansville and Indianapolis: Evansville – Terre Haute
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=NYC (today’s Indiana Southern Railroad and its abandoned sections) through Oakland City, Washington, Elnora and Worthington. Traced length 133.7 mi against the ICC valuation’s 133.77 mi of main line. WARNING: a 22.8 km (14.2 mi) leg between Worthington and Jasonville is a STRAIGHT LINE — that stretch of grade is not mapped in OSM. Remaining bridges are 4.4 km or less. The Evansville end uses the C&EI alignment the E&I actually entered town on under trackage rights. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 11 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: Incorporated 7 November 1885 from three predecessors, about 60 mi of it laid on the abandoned Wabash and Erie Canal towpath. Entered Evansville over roughly 4 mi of C&EI track under trackage rights. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1885 incorporation, mileage and the C&EI trackage rights, from the ICC valuation.

segments.note: Controlled by the C&EI, which owned the entire capital stock and operated it as agent from 1911. Sold to the Big Four in 1920 and renamed the Evansville, Indianapolis and Terre Haute. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: C&EI control from 1911; 1920 sale to the Big Four.

properties.line: Peoria, Decatur and Evansville: Evansville – Olney
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=IC (today’s Indiana Southwestern Railway and abandoned grade) through Stewartsville, Poseyville, Browns and Grayville. Traced length 68.1 mi Evansville to Olney; largest straight-line bridge 4.57 km, at the collapsed Wabash River crossing near Grayville. Drawn only as far as Olney: the PD&E continued via Newton, Mattoon and Decatur to Peoria, but that grade was lifted and is not in OSM, so it is not drawn rather than approximated.
properties.speed_source: Estimated for an 1880s branch; no timetable consulted.

segments.note: Completed Parkersburg to Evansville in 1881, giving Evansville a through route to Decatur and Peoria. Bankrupt and sold at auction to the Illinois Central, which leased it from 1 September 1900. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1881 completion and the 1900 sale/1 September 1900 IC lease.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=IC (today’s Indiana Southwestern Railway and abandoned grade) through Stewartsville, Poseyville, Browns and Grayville. Traced length 68.1 mi Evansville to Olney; largest straight-line bridge 4.57 km, at the collapsed Wabash River crossing near Grayville. Drawn only as far as Olney: the PD&E continued via Newton, Mattoon and Decatur to Peoria, but that grade was lifted and is not in OSM, so it is not drawn rather than approximated.

segments.note: Illinois Central, by lease from 1 September 1900 and by conveyance from 8 April 1905. THE 1938 END YEAR IS NOT SOURCED FOR THIS SEGMENT — see metadata.not_yet_sourced. Headway estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the IC lease and conveyance dates are sourced; the end of passenger service is not. Sources place the last passenger train on the Peoria–Decatur–Mattoon end of the PD&E in the "late 1930s"; 1938 is a reading of that phrase applied to the Evansville end, and is unverified.

properties.company: Cleveland, Cincinnati, Chicago and St. Louis Railway
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=NYC north-west of Evansville, 34.0 mi to Mount Carmel, Illinois. Largest straight-line bridge 3.9 km, on the section Conrail abandoned north of Evansville toward Skelton, which is only partly mapped. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 10 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: The Evansville, Mount Carmel and Northern opened in July 1911 as a Big Four subsidiary, running northwest out of Evansville along Pigeon Creek. At its peak it carried a through sleeper to Chicago. Passenger service was discontinued in 1942. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: July 1911 opening as a Big Four subsidiary and the 1942 end of passenger service.
